title: Braille grew out of ‘night writing’, a 12-dot code pitched for soldiers in the dark

cover.alt: A fingertip resting on a white page of embossed braille, the raised dots lit from the side so they cast small shadows.

body: Charles Barbier’s tactile code used sets of 12 raised dots to stand for 36 different sounds. It got the name ‘night writing’ when it was considered as a way for soldiers to communicate silently without a light. It had three problems: its symbols stood for sounds rather than letters, a 12-dot symbol would not fit under the pad of a reading finger, and it had no numbers or punctuation. In 1824 Louis Braille, aged 15 and blind since a childhood accident, fixed all three. He shrank the cell to six dots, two columns of three, gave each letter its own pattern, added numerals and punctuation, and published his system in 1829.

left.label: Night writing
left.text: 12-dot symbols for 36 sounds. Too big for one fingertip, and no numbers or punctuation.

right.label: Braille, 1824
right.text: 6-dot cells, one pattern per letter, plus numerals and punctuation. One cell fits under the finger.

slides.question: A braille cell has six dot positions. How many different patterns are possible, counting the blank one used for a space?
slides.explanation: 64: each of the six positions is either raised or flat, and the pattern with no dots at all marks a space between words.

steps.label: a to j: patterns in the top four dots
k to t: the same, plus dot 3
u, v, x, y, z: plus dots 3 and 6

slides.alt: An antique black and brass braille typewriter with six wooden keys and a space bar, a wooden roller and a curved handle.
slides.caption: The Hall Braille writer of 1892, an early mechanical machine for typing braille, invented by Frank H. Hall.

slides.question: Braille has no separate shapes for digits. What stands for the numbers 1 to 9 and 0?
slides.explanation: The first ten letters double as the ten digits, in an alphabetic numeral system. The finger reads one cell at a time.
